quick: 10 mg three times daily before meals (max 30 mg/day), shortest duration (typically <=1 week)
Avoid unless clearly necessary - limited data
Small amounts in milk; sometimes used off-label as galactagogue with caution
Caution / reduce frequency in severe impairment
ECG/QT and electrolytes in at-risk patients; cardiac risk factors
summary: Domperidone is a peripheral dopamine D2 antagonist used as an antiemetic and prokinetic for nausea, vomiting, and dyspepsia/gastroparesis. It does not readily cross the blood-brain barrier, so it causes fewer central extrapyramidal effects than metoclopramide, but it can prolong the QT interval and cause serious arrhythmias. It is NOT FDA-approved (EMA-restricted; available in many countries) - this record is from EMA/SmPC and BNF sources and is PENDING CLINICAL REVIEW.
indications: Dyspepsia / functional gastrointestinal symptoms and gastroparesis (per regional approvals)
Off-label: stimulation of lactation (galactagogue) - not an approved indication

dosage.r: Adult and adolescent >=12 yr and >=35 kg
dosage.d: 10 mg up to three times daily
dosage.n: Maximum 30 mg/day; use lowest effective dose for shortest time (usually <=1 week)

dosage.d: 0.25 mg/kg up to three times daily
dosage.n: Max 0.75 mg/kg/day; restricted use per regional guidance

admin: Take 15-30 minutes before meals (and at bedtime if needed) - absorption is reduced by food/gastric acid
Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration
Do not exceed 30 mg/day in adults
Review the need for continued use regularly
moa: Blocks peripheral dopamine D2 receptors in the gastrointestinal tract and the chemoreceptor trigger zone (which lies outside the blood-brain barrier). This enhances gastric and upper GI motility, increases lower esophageal sphincter tone, and produces an antiemetic effect, with minimal central CNS penetration.

absolute: Known QT prolongation / significant electrolyte disturbance / underlying cardiac disease such as heart failure
Concomitant QT-prolonging drugs or potent CYP3A4 inhibitors
GI hemorrhage, mechanical obstruction, or perforation

preg: Avoid unless clearly necessary; human data are limited and there is potential for fetal cardiac (QT) effects. Use only if the benefit justifies the risk.
lact: Excreted into breast milk in small amounts (infant exposure typically <0.1% of weight-adjusted maternal dose). Sometimes used off-label to promote lactation, but this is unapproved and must be weighed against maternal cardiac (QT) risk.
renal: In severe renal impairment, reduce dosing frequency (e.g., once or twice daily) and consider dose reduction, since the elimination half-life is prolonged. Repeated dosing requires caution.
hepatic: Contraindicated in moderate-to-severe hepatic impairment because domperidone is extensively hepatically metabolized. Use is acceptable in mild impairment with caution.

major: Potent CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, erythromycin, clarithromycin, ritonavir - raise domperidone levels and QT risk) - contraindicated
Other QT-prolonging drugs (antiarrhythmics, certain antipsychotics, methadone) - contraindicated/avoid
moderate: Drugs causing hypokalemia (diuretics - increase arrhythmia risk)
minor: Antacids/antisecretory drugs (reduce absorption - do not take at the same time)
interactions.food: Take before meals; food and reduced gastric acid lower absorption

serious: QT prolongation and serious ventricular arrhythmia / sudden cardiac death
rare: Extrapyramidal effects (rare; mainly if BBB compromised, e.g., infants)
emergency: Ventricular arrhythmia / torsades de pointes / cardiac arrest

monitoring: ECG/QT interval in patients with cardiac risk factors or on interacting drugs
counsel: Use for the shortest time possible and do not exceed the prescribed dose
Stop and seek urgent care for palpitations, fainting, or irregular heartbeat
Tell your doctor about heart problems and all other medicines (some combinations are dangerous)
Note: this medicine is not FDA-approved - follow local prescribing guidance
pk: Supports dosing up to three times daily
Store at room temperature, below 25-30 C; protect from light
pearls: Poor blood-brain-barrier penetration means fewer central extrapyramidal effects than metoclopramide
EMA restricted use to nausea/vomiting at low dose/short duration due to cardiac (QT) risk; NOT FDA-approved
Avoid with QT-prolonging drugs and potent CYP3A4 inhibitors
Off-label use as a galactagogue is common but unapproved and not without cardiac risk
missed: Take the missed dose before your next meal if you remember in time; otherwise skip it and resume the usual schedule. Do not double the dose or exceed 30 mg in a day.
overdose: Overdose may cause drowsiness, disorientation, extrapyramidal reactions, and QT prolongation/arrhythmia. Management is supportive with ECG monitoring; anticholinergic or antiparkinsonian drugs may help extrapyramidal symptoms. There is no specific antidote.
